cover.description: A themed title page; optional subtitle, logo and metadata collapse when omitted.

running-head.description: Document title in the header and confidentiality, page fields and date in the footer, inherited by every later section; those sections continue on the page.

key-takeaways.description: Executive conclusions with bounded one-line takeaways. Copy and adapt this document-local example.

source-line.description: A hairline and a source line in the source role, under a figure or a table. The data blocks invoke it; copy it to add a source to anything else.

kpi-row.description: Two to four headline metrics in equal columns: value with its unit, label, and a signed delta with a direction glyph; four of them set the figures a size smaller. An optional source collapses with its hairline. Text budgets reject overflow; columns reflow at unchanged type size.

unit.description: Suffix drawn after the figure at half its size: %, €m, pts. Write the space yourself when one belongs.

delta.description: Signed change shown beside the figure: +3.2 pts, −0.4.

trend.description: Direction glyph drawn before the delta.

figure-caption.description: The numbered caption under a figure: **Figure N.** and the text, N being a Word SEQ field over the figure sequence. chart-figure and figure invoke it, so charts and images number together.

chart-figure.description: A numbered, sourced chart: the chart itself (highcharts through the export server, or a native chart on the office-open renderer), a caption that says what it shows, an optional takeaway beneath, and the source line the report cites. The source is required; the figure number is a Word SEQ field.

chart.description: A highcharts or chart component. Put the unit in the value-axis title: Revenue (€m).

caption.description: What the chart shows, as a statement: Revenue by quarter, 2026.

takeaway.description: The one sentence the reader should leave with.

data-table.description: A sourced numeric table: a title, a text column of row labels at a fifth of the measure, one to five data columns right-aligned by construction, then optional notes and a source line. With its header, 24 rows keep the table on one page; the table-design rule checks the compiled table for mixed decimals.

labels.description: Row labels, top to bottom. Every data column lists its cells in this order and at this count.

header.description: Column header; put the unit here: Revenue (€m).

cells.description: One formatted value per row label, rounded the same way down the column.

numeric.description: Right-align header and cells so digits line up by place value. Set false for a text column.

notes.description: What the reader needs to interpret the figures: definitions, periods, exclusions.

callout.description: An aside set off by a hairline rule down its left edge: a short label over up to sixty words of text. No fill, so it reads as a note beside the argument rather than a box in it.

footnotes.description: Notes and sources: every distinct source-role slot value the document's block invocations carry, in order, as a numbered list under a label — the engine's /sources context. Emits nothing when no invocation cites a source.

slots.title: Post-Merger Integration Assessment
slots.subtitle: Depot Network Consolidation and Synergy Capture

slots.title: Synergy is real but two-fifths depends on an unbudgeted system

items: Customer overlap is 31% and depot overlap is 12 of 41 sites, so this is a selective integration, not a network merger.
The EUR8.2m annual synergy is real, but 40% of it (EUR3.3m) requires one dispatch system neither company has funded.
Recommend approving the dispatch migration business case in the first quarter, in parallel with quick-win synergies, not after them.

slots.source: Source: Integration business case model, September 2026

props.text: The combined footprint spans 41 depots across both networks, with 12 sites — 29% of the total — operated by both companies today; the remaining 29 depots are complementary and extend coverage rather than duplicate it. Customer overlap sits at 31%, meaning most of the acquired book is incremental revenue, but the shared third of the customer base carries the near-term risk of visible service disruption during integration. Because the overlap is partial rather than total, the sequencing question is not whether to merge networks but which synergies can be captured immediately and which must wait on shared infrastructure.

slots.title: The remaining 40% of synergy is locked behind one system

props.text: Of the EUR8.2m annual run-rate identified in due diligence, EUR4.9m (60%) comes from procurement consolidation, overlapping-depot rationalization and contract harmonization on the shared customer base; none of it depends on new systems, and all of it is achievable within eighteen months on the infrastructure each company already runs. The remaining EUR3.3m (40%) comes from cross-fleet dispatching and route optimization across all 41 depots, which is only possible once both companies operate a single dispatch platform. Today they operate two, and neither company's budget currently funds the migration between them.

slots.caption: Synergy run-rate on schedule versus a one-year deferral of the dispatch migration
slots.takeaway: A twelve-month delay in approving the dispatch migration pushes full EUR8.2m run-rate capture from month twenty-four to month thirty-six.
slots.source: Source: Integration business case model, September 2026

props.text: The gap between the two lines is the cost of sequencing this wrong: the synergy does not disappear, but a year of it is never recovered, since run-rate not captured in a given year cannot be captured retroactively. Approving the migration business case in the first quarter, in parallel with the quick-win tracks, is what keeps the combined business on the faster line.

slots.title: Recommended sequence: fund the migration in month one

props.text: The sequence follows the money: capture the EUR4.9m that needs no new system first, while treating the dispatch migration as a funded Day-1 workstream rather than a Year-2 idea. Three tracks run in parallel from kickoff — quick-win synergies, the dispatch system decision and migration, and organizational integration for the 31% of customers served by both companies — because running the system track after the quick wins, rather than alongside them, is what turns a twelve-month delay into a permanent loss of value.

items: Stand up the joint Integration Management Office and steering committee cadence.
Approve the dispatch-system business case and secure funding neither company has budgeted today.
Finalize the consolidation plan for the 12 overlapping depots — leases, headcount and assets.
Launch combined procurement for fleet, consumables and sub-contracted labor.
Begin contract harmonization and a retention program for the 31% of customers served by both companies.
Execute depot consolidation across the 12 overlapping sites; onboard the remaining 29 depots onto shared back-office processes.
Begin dispatch-system data migration and pilot it on the overlapping depot cluster.
Reach roughly EUR4.9m of annualized run-rate from procurement, depots and contracts — the system-independent 60%.
Close the customer retention program for the overlapping segment and open cross-sell into the acquired book.
Cut over all 41 depots to the single dispatch platform.
Bring cross-fleet dispatching and route optimization live, starting to realize the system-dependent EUR3.3m.
Confirm the EUR4.9m system-independent run-rate is fully locked in and stable.
Run a post-migration stabilization review with the steering committee.

slots.title: Cumulative synergy run-rate against the EUR8.2m target
slots.notes: Run-rate is the annualized value of synergies live at each checkpoint, not cash captured to date; the system-dependent EUR3.3m begins contributing only after the Month 18 dispatch cutover.
slots.source: Source: Integration business case model, September 2026

slots.label: Why month one matters
slots.text: Dispatch migrations typically take twelve to eighteen months from budget approval to cutover. Approve it in month one and the EUR3.3m system-dependent synergy stays on the same clock as the rest of the integration; approve it in month twelve and full run-rate capture slips to month thirty-six, forfeiting roughly a year of that value permanently.

slots.title: Deferring the migration a year is a permanent loss, not a delay

props.text: Deferring the dispatch-system business case by a year does not just delay EUR3.3m of synergy — it forfeits it. The system-dependent tranche only exists once cross-fleet dispatching is live across all 41 depots; a year spent running two dispatch systems in parallel is a year the combined network never gets back, so the loss compounds rather than merely shifts. Beyond the direct EUR3.3m, deferral means paying for two dispatch platforms and their support teams for an extra year, carrying the 31% overlapping customer base through a second season of inconsistent service, and negotiating the migration budget a year later with less leverage and a business case that has to be re-sold to a steering committee that will reasonably ask why it was not approved the first time. The recommendation to this committee is straightforward: approve the dispatch migration funding alongside the quick-win synergies this quarter, not after them.
